notes: REBUILD of claude-for-artificial-intelligence/claude-liam-bs-01-pick-and-scope. The source episode's core craft is kept — bounding a role description to one job, and the closest-job test — and this film hands both to the viewer as its own deliverable. See PEDAGOGY.md for the six places the episode can be strengthened.

Builder changed from `ai-explainer` (one tight insight) to `deep-explainer`: this film carries a framework, two published sources, a reversal, and an original measurement. The source README scopes deep-explainer at 5-10 minutes.

NO POINT VALUE from the INFO 7375 assignment appears anywhere, spoken or on screen. The source episode's figures for the rubric could not be confirmed against any reachable primary source, and course figures date quickly, so they are left out rather than risked. Author decision 2026-08-18.
Title names the SUBJECT per PLAYBOOK 1c; the method phrase 'The Four Questions' is kept in metadata rather than the title.
PROOF Phase 2 gate: the four-question board lands at B01B (~18s), ahead of any example.

C1 fix (PROOF review): the 71.6/68.0/66.3 figures appear ONLY in B06, scoped to expertise-claim personas. B11 must never import them as a reason to tighten a task-context statement - that is the exact conflation this film exposes.
B10 reports disagreement rates only. Correctness rates are excluded: revision 2 established they measure the author's item-writing, not the models. See EXPERIMENT.md.
RUNTIME RISK: estimated ~9-10 min. See PROOF-REVIEW.md cut order. B08's silence and B10's bound are protected from cuts.

VOICE: am_onyx (Onyx). The toolkit's generate_audio_kokoro.py enforces ALLOWED_VOICES={am_onyx, af_bella} and REJECTS af_kore, despite all 50 Kokoro voices being present in voices-v1.0.bin. The repo README's Kore/af_kore default cannot be rendered by this toolkit. Onyx chosen for the narration register (this film is a first-person investigation, not a lesson). Documented departure, same as Film 4.

INTRO SUMMARY: B01B is an explicit roadmap per PLAYBOOK 1 ('build in an intro-summary beat by default'). It states what the video covers before any specifics, and carries the four-question graphic that satisfies the PROOF Phase 2 gate.

BRAND: began as brand=claude-liam + folderLabel=@HumanitariansAI, carried over from the source folder name; beat_lint rule 7 flagged the combination as inconsistent. claude-liam binds to kicker 'Computational Skepticism' + chip @NikBearBrown. Switched to claude-hai, whose chip (@HumanitariansAI), voice (am_onyx) and register (Pragmatist) all match this film. Deciding factor: the narration says 'from Humanitarians AI', so a @NikBearBrown chip would contradict the spoken words.
`topic` is NOT a per-video description — beat_lint rule 7 requires it to EQUAL the fixed per-channel series kicker. The descriptive line now lives in `subject_line`.

B13 uses ClaudeTitleOutroFull, a resolution-scaling variant of ClaudeTitleOutro. The shared ClaudeTitleOutro sizes in absolute pixels (fontSize 72, maxWidth 1080) tuned for 1080p, so at 2160p it filled only 15% of the safe area — the emptiest frame in the film and the last one a viewer sees. Measured on isolated stills: 15% -> 33% (height-relative sizing) -> 78% (space-between instead of centred). Shared component left untouched; the absolute-pixel scaling issue affects ClaudeWindow and ClaudeVerdictArtifact too and is a toolkit-level fix to raise, not to patch unilaterally.

NARRATION REWRITE 2026-08-18 (author direction at Gate P): (1) the on-screen/spoken persona is Tanmay Kulkarni from Humanitarians AI, not Onyx — matching Week 17's `voice: TanmayKulkarni` + `voice_kokoro: am_onyx` convention, where the film is the fellow's and Kokoro delivers it; (2) plain-language pass across all 17 beats so a general audience can follow. Jargon removed: instrument, exclude/exclusion, persona, task-context, expertise depth, conceptual/explanatory questions, nearest neighbour -> 'closest job', preprint now explained inline as 'other researchers haven't checked it yet'. Every number, source and stated limit is unchanged.

GATE P REVISION 1 (author read-aloud, 2026-08-18): (1) duplicate greeting removed from B01 — B00 already introduces the presenter; (2) B10 now sets up what the experiment tested and why before any number, instead of opening on figures; (3) TONE TOWARD THE SOURCE MATERIAL softened throughout per author direction — the exercise is framed as sound practice with room to be strengthened, not as defective. B02 'those blanks are an admission' -> 'those blanks are honest'; B08 'never separates' -> 'doesn't ask', and the gap reframed as good news; B09 now calls the instruction 'genuinely useful' before questioning how much weight to give the AI's answer; B11 'had the advice right and never checked why' -> 'where it could be stronger is spelling out the reason - something to add, not to replace'. The only sharp criticism left in the film is of the author's own pharmacist example, which is the point of B04B.

SHOW-PASS FIXES 2026-08-18 (first review on real 4K frames): (1) all four ClaudeComposerAsk beats were rendering the component's default folderLabel '@NikBearBrown' while the narration says 'Humanitarians AI' — folderLabel is a per-beat prop and was never passed; now '@HumanitariansAI' on B00/B01/B09/B12. (2) The plain-language pass had only touched narration_text, leaving on-screen card copy in the original jargon (exclude / nearest neighbour / load-bearing phrase / verdict), so cards contradicted the spoken words. PLAYBOOK §1 warns about exactly this: a pass that only scans narration misses claims sitting in a visual-card prop. Card copy now matches the narration.

GATE V CLEANUP: B02/B04 (was ClaudeWindow, 18-20% fill) and B06/B10 (was ClaudeVerdictArtifact, 53%) now use ClaudeArtifactCardFull, one component with a `chrome` mode covering both looks. Root cause in both originals was absolute-pixel sizing — ClaudeWindow hardcodes width:1100, which is 57% of a 1920 frame but 29% of a 3840 one. Correct at 1080p, under-filled at 2160p. Originals left untouched; this is additive.

B06 card: our own labels say 'personality' to match the narration; line 4 keeps 'persona' because it is a VERBATIM QUOTE from arXiv 2603.18507 and is shown in quotation marks. Rewording a quote to match house vocabulary would be a factcheck violation.

TERMINOLOGY DRIFT FIX 2026-08-18 (PROOF Phase 3 punch list item 1): card copy on B05/B08/B10/B10B still read 'the model', 'neighbour', 'statements' while the narration said 'the AI', 'closest job', 'descriptions'. Root cause of the earlier miss: these components apply textTransform:uppercase, so the STORED prop values are sentence case while my swap keys were ALL CAPS — nothing matched, and my verification grep looked for 'nearest neighbour' rather than bare 'neighbour', so it reported clean. Checked a representation instead of the artifact, twice in one pass.

beats.narration_text: Hi, this is Tanmay Kulkarni from Humanitarians AI.

props.topic: HUMANITARIANS AI · DESCRIBING YOUR OWN ROLE PRECISELY ENOUGH FOR AI

beats.act: cold open — subject in plain words
beats.narration_text: The hard part of using AI isn't saying what you want. It's saying who you are. Every template you'll ever pick up was written for a generic professional, and you're not one. So this video is about a single skill: describing your own job clearly enough that the answer you get back is actually about your job.

props.topic: HUMANITARIANS AI · DESCRIBING YOUR OWN ROLE
props.command: The hard part isn't what you want. It's who you are.

beats.act: intro summary — what this video covers
beats.narration_text: Here's what we'll cover. First, four questions you can run on any description you write. Then what the research actually says about telling AI who you are — which is less than you'd hope. Then a test I ran, four hundred and eighty times, because one of those four questions turned out to matter far more than the other three.
beats.gate_note: PROOF Phase 2: the framework GRAPHIC lands here, ~18s in, ahead of any example. B03 unpacks it.

props.boardKicker: Run them in order on any description you write.

questions.q: Does it rule anyone out, or just describe you?
questions.fails: True of you, and of the person at the next desk.

questions.q: Who has the closest job to yours?
questions.fails: Pick someone far away and you pass for free.

questions.q: Which words rule that person out?
questions.fails: Can't point at them — it's just long.

questions.q: Would someone else agree with you?
questions.fails: If only you can run it, it's an opinion.

beats.narration_text: Open most AI exercises and you'll find the same shape. A paragraph with blanks in it. Your role goes here. Your task goes here. Your limits, your format, the people who depend on the answer. Those blanks are honest — whoever wrote the exercise can't know who you are, so they leave you room to say it. The interesting question is what you put in them. Watch what most people write in that first blank: healthcare professional. Software engineer. Financial analyst. Those aren't jobs. They're categories — and a category gets you a category-shaped answer.
beats.tts_note: Two deliberate hard stops in the category list. Verify both in the silencedetect sweep; if either gap exceeds ~0.6s, join with commas and lose the effect rather than ship a hole.

props.artifactHeading: A paragraph with brackets in it

beats.narration_text: So here are the four questions. Run them in order, on any description you write. First: does it rule anyone out, or does it just describe you? Most of what people write is true of them, and just as true of the person at the next desk. Describing yourself is easy. Ruling other people out is the work. Second: who has the closest job to yours? Not someone in another department — the person whose work is most like yours. Pick someone far away and you'll pass without learning anything. Third: which exact words rule that person out? Point at them. If you can't point at them, your description isn't specific. It's just long. Fourth: would someone else agree with you? If you're the only person who can run your own test and get your own answer, that isn't a test. It's an opinion. The order matters. The first two are quick, and they catch most weak descriptions. The third is the one people skip. And the fourth turned out to matter far more than I expected.
beats.tts_note: Ordinals with colons — First: Second: Third: Fourth: — never 'One. Two. Three.' per PLAYBOOK 1d, which would insert hard stops long enough to hear as dropped words.

props.boardKicker: The first two are quick. The third gets skipped. The fourth is the one that catches you.

questions.fails: Pick someone far away and you pass for free.

questions.q: Which words rule that person out?
questions.fails: Can't point at them — it's just long.

questions.q: Would someone else agree with you?
questions.fails: If only you can run it, it's an opinion.

beats.act: worked example — questions one to three
beats.narration_text: Let's actually run it. Here's a description: a hospital pharmacist working nights, who checks discharge medicines against a safety list called the Beers Criteria before the patient goes home. Question one — does it rule anyone out? It definitely describes somebody. Whether it rules anyone out is what we don't know yet, and that's the whole question. Question two: who has the closest job? Not a radiologist. Not a hospital manager. The night nurse on the same ward — same hours, same patients, same discharge. She's who we test against. Question three: which words could that nurse not write? Working nights — she works nights too. Before the patient goes home — she's standing right there for it. But checking medicines against the Beers Criteria? That's the pharmacist's expertise. Those are the words doing the work.
beats.gate_note: The candidate load-bearing phrase must be legible and visibly marked at the moment it is named.

artifactLines: Clinical pharmacist on night shift —— she works nights too.
…before the patient leaves the unit —— she's there for that.
…verifies discharge medication orders against Beers Criteria —— the words doing the work?

beats.narration_text: Good. Except now question four. Would someone else agree? So I looked it up. And the Beers Criteria — the actual document — was written by a panel of doctors, pharmacists, and nurses. A nursing institute publishes it. In a series made for nurses. Described as a tool to help nurses review medicines. She could write those words. She probably has. My example fails. The line I was confident about, the one I'd have put on a slide, rules nobody out — and I only found that out because question four made me check something other than my own opinion. If you want words that really do rule her out, it isn't the safety list. It's who signs off: releasing the prescription in the pharmacy system before it can be handed over. She checks it. He releases it. That's the line. Notice how that went. Questions one to three were me marking my own homework, and I passed. Question four was the only one that could catch me — and it's the one most advice quietly skips.
beats.gate_note: PRODUCTION GATE: the AGS panel composition AND the HIGN nursing-series attribution must both be legible at the moment the reversal is stated. Held >=2s.
beats.tts_note: 'She could write that phrase. She probably has.' — the silence between these two short sentences is doing the work. Do not join them. 'She reviews. He releases.' stays clipped. Both clusters go in the silencedetect sweep.

props.splitTitle: Question four: would a stranger agree?
props.leftBody: "Verifying orders against Beers Criteria is the pharmacist's expertise."
props.leftNote: Confident. Unchecked. I'd have put it on a slide.
props.rightBody: AGS 2023 Beers Criteria: written by a 12-member panel of medicine, nursing, and pharmacy. Published by the Hartford Institute for Geriatric Nursing — in a series for nurses.
props.rightNote: "assists nurses and interprofessional team members in medication reviews"
props.footer: Those words rule nobody out. Question four is the only one that could catch that.

beats.act: the split — two things, one name
beats.narration_text: Here's what I'd been missing, and it's why this is harder than it looks. There are two completely different things people mean by telling AI who you are, and nobody separates them. The first is a claim about the AI. You are a senior hospital pharmacist with fifteen years of experience. You're telling it who to pretend to be. The second describes your situation. Night shift. Discharge medicines. Before the patient goes home. You're not claiming anything about the AI — you're telling it where you're standing. Same trick, same name, in every guide you'll read. Two completely different things. And only one of them has actually been tested.
beats.gate_note: PRODUCTION GATE: both kinds on screen TOGETHER, held >=2s. The comparator mounts both columns on one shared spring for exactly this reason.

props.leftBody: "You are a senior clinical pharmacist with fifteen years of experience."
props.leftNote: Telling it who to pretend to be.
props.rightBody: "Night shift. Discharge orders. Before the patient walks out."
props.rightNote: Telling it where you are standing.
props.footer: Same technique. Same name. Two different mechanisms.

beats.narration_text: The first kind — the you-are-an-expert kind — has been tested, and the results aren't flattering. One team gave an AI expert personalities and then ran it through a general knowledge test. With no personality, it scored seventy-one point six percent. Add a short expert personality: sixty-eight. Add a long, detailed one: sixty-six point three. Their words, not mine: longer personality prompts do more damage. So the thing everyone does — piling on job titles, years of experience, specialities — cost accuracy on that test. And the more they piled on, the more it cost. This is a preprint, which means other researchers haven't checked it yet. I'm telling you that because it matters.
beats.gate_note: PRODUCTION GATE: the three numbers and the PREPRINT label in frame together, with the paper title.
beats.source: Hu, Rostami & Thomason, 'Expert Personas Improve LLM Alignment but Damage Accuracy', arXiv 2603.18507, March 2026, Figure 1b. PREPRINT.

artifactLines: Not peer reviewed. Measured on “you are an expert” personalities only.

beats.narration_text: A second group asked a narrower question: when does it help? They found a trade, not an improvement. Telling the AI who to be made answers deeper. It also made them less clear. Where it helped: questions asking for advice, in medicine and psychology. Where plain asking won: questions asking it to explain something, in finance, law, science and technology. Also a preprint. A made-up test set, only a few AI models, and the marking was done by another AI — the authors say so themselves.
beats.gate_note: PRODUCTION GATE: helped-domains and hurt-domains on screen TOGETHER, held >=2s. Stated limitations appear WITH the findings, not after.
beats.source: Xiao et al., 'When Does Persona Prompting Actually Help?', arXiv 2605.29420, 28 May 2026. PREPRINT.

props.splitTitle: A trade, not an improvement — PREPRINT arXiv 2605.29420
props.rightBody: Conceptual and explanatory questions, in finance, legal, science, technology.
props.footer: Synthetic benchmark · limited model set · graded by another model — the authors' own stated limits.

beats.narration_text: So I went looking for a study on the second kind. The situation kind. The one the exercise actually asks you to write. I couldn't find one. And that second paper measures every expert personality as one thing — it doesn't ask whether the answer changed because the AI was told it was an expert, or because the words described the job differently. Every test I could find is of the first kind. Which means the advice isn't wrong. It just hasn't been tested yet. Those are very different things, and the difference is good news, because untested is something any of us can go and fix.
beats.tone: deflated, then determined — the low point
beats.tts_note: PROTECTED FROM CUTS. 'It isn't there.' takes a full stop and a real pause — this is the one place in the film where silence is the content.
beats.gate_note: PRODUCTION GATE: both paper titles legible; the unmeasured half visibly marked via dimSide.

props.splitTitle: Only one half was ever measured
props.rightBody: "Night shift. Discharge orders. Before the patient walks out."
props.rightNote: No study found. This is what the assignment asks you to write.
props.footer: Not wrong. Unmeasured. Those are different things.

beats.narration_text: Which leaves you where it left me. The exercise gives you a sensible instruction: write a description of your job, hand it to an AI, and ask whether it's specific enough. And that's a genuinely useful habit. But specific enough is exactly the kind of judgement where an AI can sound completely certain and be reading something else entirely. So how much weight should you put on its answer? Both easy answers are wrong. Trust it completely, and you're trusting something nobody has tested. Refuse to use it, and you've thrown away a second pair of eyes that costs you nothing. I didn't want to guess. So I tested it.
beats.tone: unresolved — genuinely asking. Do not answer here.
beats.tts_note: A beat of silence after 'So do you use it or not?'. 'So I measured it.' is clipped — the hinge into B10.

props.greeting: So do you use it or not?
props.command: Trust it — you're trusting something nobody measured. Refuse — you've thrown away free eyes.

beats.narration_text: So here's what I did, and why. If the advice is to hand your description to an AI and let it name the closest job, then the whole thing rests on the AI giving you a steady answer. So that's what I measured. I wrote twenty-four job descriptions across healthcare, finance and engineering — some deliberately sharp, some deliberately vague. Then I asked two AI models the same question about each one, five separate times. Four hundred and eighty answers in total. Here's the first thing that came back. Ask an AI who has the closest job to yours, five times over, and you get roughly two and a half different answers. Seventy-nine percent of descriptions got more than one answer from the first model. Seventy-one percent from the second. Not different wording. Different jobs.
beats.tone: the second reveal — measured, not breathless
beats.gate_note: PRODUCTION GATE: the distinct-neighbour numbers legible at render size.
beats.source: Our own measurement. results-20260818T04*.json ships with the film.
beats.tts_note: 'Not different wording. Different professions.' — the film's sharpest pair. Keep clipped.

props.artifactHeading: Ask five times, get ~2.5 different jobs
artifactLines: Haiku 4.5 — 79% of descriptions got more than one job (mean 2.25)
Sonnet 5 — 71% of descriptions got more than one job (mean 2.46)
Picked the same job title: 15% / 9% — not a different job at all

beats.narration_text: And because the pass-or-fail depends on which job it picked, that moves too. On the first model, forty-two percent of descriptions got both a pass and a fail — same AI, same question, nothing changed but the attempt. Then the useful part. Stop asking the AI to pick the closest job. Tell it. Name that person yourself, and the flip-flopping drops by about two and a half times. Forty-two percent down to seventeen. Seventeen down to eight. The two models agreeing with each other goes from sixty-seven percent up to eighty-eight. One sentence of change. A steadier test. Now the limits, because they matter. Twenty-four descriptions, two models, one task, and I wrote the descriptions myself. This doesn't show AI is bad at this. It shows the answer moves — and that where it moves is something you control.
beats.tone: useful, then cooling into the bound
beats.tts_note: PROTECTED FROM CUTS — the bound paragraph. Slows noticeably; this is the cooling beat after the peak (PLAYBOOK 1a).
beats.gate_note: PRODUCTION GATE: 42%->17% and 17%->8% pairs in frame TOGETHER, held >=2s. The bound appears WITH the finding, not after it.
beats.excluded: No correctness rates. Those measure the author's item-writing, not the models — see EXPERIMENT.md revision 2.

props.leftLabel: Ask the AI to pick the closest job
props.leftNote: The two AI models agreed with each other 67% of the time.
props.rightLabel: Tell the AI which job is closest
props.rightNote: The two AI models agreed with each other 88% of the time.
props.footer: Bound: 24 descriptions, 2 models, one task, and I wrote the descriptions. This does not show models are bad at this — it shows the answer moves, and where it moves is yours to control.

beats.narration_text: So the advice was right. Tighten the description until it fits one person. Keep doing that. But it's worth being clear about why it works. Not because being specific is obviously better, and — careful here — not because of those accuracy numbers either. Those were measured on the other kind, the you-are-an-expert kind. Borrowing them would be me making the exact mistake I've just spent four minutes describing. Tighten it for the reason question three gives you: words you can't point at aren't doing any work. And run the closest-job test, because it steadies things — as long as you pick that person, instead of asking an AI to pick for you. That part I did test. So the exercise gives you good practice. Where it could be stronger is spelling out the reason — and that's something to add, not something to replace. It's exactly what happened to my own pharmacist example four minutes ago.
beats.tone: convinced, calm — resolution. Warm, not triumphant.
beats.gate_note: PRODUCTION GATE: the advice kept and the reason corrected in frame TOGETHER, held >=2s.
beats.c1_note: C1 FIX: this beat must NOT cite 71.6/66.3. It names the temptation and refuses it out loud, because importing the expertise-claim number here would commit the film's own error.

props.splitTitle: The practice survives. The reason changes.
props.leftLabel: Keep — what the exercise got right
props.leftBody: Tighten the description until it fits one person. Run the closest-job test.
props.leftNote: Sound craft. Nothing measured argues against it.
props.rightLabel: Change — the reason, and one method
props.rightBody: Not "specific is better." A phrase you can't point at isn't doing work — and YOU pick the closest job, not the AI.
props.rightNote: The accuracy numbers belong to the other kind. Borrowing them would repeat the mistake.
props.footer: Practice right, mechanism unexamined — the most ordinary thing in technical writing.

beats.narration_text: Your turn, and this is four steps, not something to paste. First: write your job description. Second: name the person whose job is closest to yours — closest, not furthest. If you're reaching for someone in another department, you've picked wrong. Third: underline the one phrase that person could not write. Fourth, and this is the one: delete that phrase and read it again. If it still sounds fine, it was never specific. It was just long. You've done it right if you find a description you were happy with and can't point to the words doing the work. You've done it wrong if everything passes first try — that means you marked yourself generously, or you picked someone who was never really close. And if you do hand it to an AI: tell it who that person is. Don't ask.
beats.tts_note: Ordinals with colons per PLAYBOOK 1d. 'Don't ask.' lands hard — last line before the outro.
